# Elements of Agrisolar Design {#sec-elements}

A solar project is a very long list of decisions, and almost all of them fall into five groups. Where the array goes. What gets built. What grows and how the place is run. Who holds the asset. What the parties signed. These are the **elements of agrisolar design**, and they are the only things anyone can actually change.

Everything else in this document sits on one side or the other of them. The [scale transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd) and the [sharing–sparing axis](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd) describe the hand a project was dealt. The [design pressures](3-design-pressures.qmd) are the forces arguing over what to do with it. The [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) are what comes out the far end. The five elements are the decisions in between, which is why a project can hold the same scale and the same position as its neighbor and do something completely different to the ground.

| Element | What it decides | What it can deliver |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Siting** | which ground the array takes, where on the parcel it sits, whether it stands upslope or downslope of a problem, how near it is to the fields it might serve, and whether a landscape holds a few large arrays or many small ones | water quality, habitat context, service to nearby fields |
| **Structure** | mounting type and clearance, row spacing and [ground coverage](7-terminology.qmd#term-gcr), [pore space](7-terminology.qmd#term-pore-space), [module technology](7-terminology.qmd#term-module-technology), grading and site works, and the built half of [screening](7-terminology.qmd#term-screening): berm, wall, fence line | microclimate, clearance for farming, light to the ground layer |
| **Management** | the [ground layer](7-terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer) and how it is established, the mowing and grazing calendar, [stocking density](7-terminology.qmd#term-stocking-density), [tracking and curtailment](7-terminology.qmd#term-tracking-curtailment), construction sequencing and traffic lanes, and the planted half of screening | soil and carbon, habitat, most of the water balance |
| **Ownership** | who holds the asset, decides the rest, and captures what it earns: owner-operator, landowner, developer, utility, cooperative, or shared | a share of generation revenue for the people on the ground |
| **Contracts** | lease terms and duration, offtake structure, interconnection posture, the [community-benefit](7-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) instruments, easements, and the [decommissioning](7-terminology.qmd#term-decommissioning) bond | the community function, and durability for all of the above |

: The five elements of agrisolar design. The first three act on ground and the last two act on paper. What the [scale transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) does to each of them is set out in §1.3, and it does something different to every one. {#tbl-elements}

## The three that act on ground {#sec-el-ground}

**Siting** is the choice of ground, and it is the most powerful element where a designer has it. It is also the first one to disappear. Placement decides whether a water-quality claim is even available, because the two routes want opposite ground: avoided loading needs the impaired field itself, and interception needs ground between that field and the water [@schulte2017]. It decides whether a pollinator planting reaches anyone, since a forager works a radius of roughly 1.5 km and about 3,500 km² of US farmland sits inside that distance of existing and planned facilities [@walston2018]. And it is cheaper than the argument against it usually assumes: siting New York's entire 2050 build around biodiversity came to 0.17% above the least-cost case [@gallaher2026].

**Structure** is the hardware and its geometry: mounting type, how high the modules sit, how far apart the rows run and how much of the ground they cover, and what the modules themselves are made to do. It is the element that carries the microclimate function outright, because shade, the drop in vapor-pressure deficit, and the shelter of nighttime minima are products of geometry rather than of anything growing. It also decides how much earth gets moved, which is the least visible structural decision and one of the most consequential. A mounting system that tolerates slope leaves the ground broadly as it found it, and one that needs a level plane means mass grading, so a racking choice made on cost sets the soil-carbon ledger for the next thirty years before any seed mix is chosen (§4.2). Structure is the least forgiving element for that reason. Siting and structure are both fixed on the day the project is built, and a badly sited array can sometimes be managed into usefulness, while stripped topsoil and compacted subsoil cannot be planted back.

**Management** is what grows underneath and how the place is run across its life: seed mix, establishment method, the mowing and grazing calendar, stocking density, tracking schedule, curtailment. It carries soil and carbon, most of habitat, and most of the water balance, and it is the only element that can still be changed after construction. That cuts both ways. Mowing timing is as decisive as the seed mix, because disturbance during nesting or bloom destroys the resource it was meant to supply [@blaydes2022], so a planting that was right in year one can be undone in year four by a contractor doing exactly what the maintenance schedule says.

Scale rations these three, and it rations them in opposite directions. At the farmstead, an owner has total control of the hardware and almost no choice of ground. Through the field and parcel zones, latitude opens and placement becomes the strongest instrument available. At utility scale, land assembly and grid access take the siting decision away again, and restorative practice becomes ground cover and grazing [@macknick2022; @boggis2020]. This is the [restoration mode shift](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) (§1.3), and it is the single most useful thing the transect has to say about design.

## The two that act on paper {#sec-el-paper}

**Ownership** is who holds the asset, and it settles both who has standing to decide the other four and who captures what the array earns. An owner-operator, a landowner leasing ground, a developer, a utility, a cooperative, and a set of community-solar subscribers do not want the same things, and the differences show up in the ground layer rather than only in the accounts. [Barnyard shelter solar](5-archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the clean case at the small end: it is restorative because the person who owns the array is the person who owns the animals under it, and no agreement was needed to align them.

Ownership is also the element the transect moves furthest, and it moves in one direction. At the farmstead the array belongs to the operator. Through the field and parcel zones it belongs to the landowner, or to a community-solar structure with many small holders. At landscape and regional scale it belongs to developer capital and then to a utility or an independent power producer, and the person on the ground holds a lease instead. The [lever matrix](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix) (§3.4) already records that shift as a row, and it is the row with the most riding on it.

What moves along with ownership is the generation revenue, which is the largest thing an agrisolar project creates. A lease pays for the use of ground and is not a share of what the array sells, so a landowner earning three to four times what the crop returned per acre [@sturchio2025croplands] is still being paid for land rather than for electricity. **Restorativity has an ownership question inside it**, and the size of the lease payment does not answer it. That is what makes co-ownership, community-solar subscription, and an equity stake in place of a rent restorative instruments rather than goodwill: they are the means of keeping some part of the generation revenue with the people who host the thing. The community and economic function is accordingly most at risk where a project is developer-owned and absentee, and most fully realized under local or shared ownership with early participation.

For most projects ownership is settled before design begins, by who has capital and who has land, and calling it an element is a claim that it *can* be designed rather than that it usually is. It also sits slightly upstream of the other four, since the owner is the party who signs the contracts and hires the mowing. Both of those are reasons to name it rather than reasons to fold it into contracts, because an element people treat as given is exactly the one worth showing them they can move.

**Contracts** are what the parties actually signed: lease terms and duration, offtake structure, interconnection posture, the tax or PILOT arrangement, community-benefit instruments, easements, and the decommissioning bond. This element carries the [community and economic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) almost by itself, and it carries something else that is easy to miss. It is what makes the other four last. A seed mix is a management decision, but whether it survives to year twenty is a lease question, and nearly 40% of Central Valley agricultural land is rented, so a conversion that sustains an owner can end the operation of the person actually farming the ground [@stid2025].

Siting narrows to nothing by A5, structure narrows to commodity, management is weak at A1, and ownership moves away from the operator the whole way up. **Contracts are the one element that holds its full range at every scale**, because a lease is a lease at eighty acres and at eight thousand, and every term in it is written by somebody. The clearest published case for the paper side runs through exactly that: federal biofuel policy has made conservation payments the less profitable option across much of the corn-ethanol acreage, and solar lease income can make a conservation practice affordable that was not affordable before [@sturchio2025croplands]. No ground was chosen and no hardware was changed. The restoration happened in a contract, which is the element most often left on the table.

## Which element did the work {#sec-el-mode}

Naming the elements makes a question askable that is otherwise vague: when a project turns out to be restorative, which element did it? The answer is the project's [restoration mode](7-terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode), and the sketched [archetypes](5-archetypes.qmd#sec-further-types) already carry it as a third tag alongside a scale zone and a sharing position. [Solar prairie strips](5-archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) are siting-led, because the restorative work is done by putting the planting where the runoff already goes. Regenerative solar grazing is management-led. Barnyard shelter is structure-led, and the community function is contract-led.

The mode is worth stating because it tells a reader what to copy. A design that worked because of where it sat will not transfer to a site without that ground, however carefully the rest is reproduced, and this is the mechanism behind [design import](7-terminology.qmd#term-design-import) (§6.3). It also tells a reader what to check. A siting-led claim is verified against a map, a structure-led claim against a drawing, a management-led claim against a maintenance schedule somebody has to keep for thirty years, and a contract-led claim against a document that can be read.

## Where the elements couple {#sec-el-coupling}

The five are separable enough to name and not separable enough to decide one at a time. Row spacing and ground layer are a single decision rather than two, because crops differ in how much shade they will trade for relief [@weselek2019]. Edge treatment is simultaneously habitat design and social-license design, and it costs land, shading, and room to farm. Grazing is a management decision that only works if the structure left clearance for the animals and the contract found somebody to keep them, which is why grazing arrangements fall apart for reasons that have nothing to do with grazing.

The couplings that matter most run from paper to ground. Management is continuous and therefore fragile, and it survives only as long as somebody is paying for it and somebody else is checking. Contracts are what make a management decision durable, and ownership is what decides whether anyone wanted it durable in the first place. A project can be sited perfectly, built correctly, and planted well, and still be gravel in fifteen years, because the elements that would have held it there were treated as paperwork rather than as design.

## Does the set hold? {#sec-el-completeness}

A set of five is only worth having if every decision a project makes lands in one of them. The test is to take the decisions this document names elsewhere, in the [design levers](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-levers) (§3.3), in the lever matrix (§3.4), and in the design dependencies listed under each [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) (§4), and see where each one falls. Most land cleanly. Four cases did not, and they are the ones worth stating, because they are where the set does work rather than just sorting.

[Screening](7-terminology.qmd#term-screening) lands in two elements at once, and that is the right answer rather than a defect. A berm, a wall, and a fence line are built and belong to structure; a hedgerow is planted, established, and kept, and belongs to management. Splitting them matters because the two halves fail differently. The berm is still there in year twenty whether or not anyone tended it, and the hedgerow is there only if somebody did. A project that promises visual mitigation and delivers it entirely in plantings has promised something with a maintenance bill attached, and the neighbor who objected is the person who finds out.

Two items in the §3.3 lever list turn out not to be elements at all. *Which ecological outcome is being aimed at* is an objective rather than a decision about the project, which makes it the [restorative goals](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) pressure. *Which regulations and certifications apply* is not chosen by anybody building, which makes it [policy and permission](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures). Both are real and both belong in §3, and a list that carries a goal and a constraint alongside seven actual choices is sorting three different kinds of thing under one heading.

Two of the definitions above had to widen to hold everything. **Structure** covers grading and site works and not only hardware, because how much earth is moved decides both where the water goes and how much soil carbon is still there to build on, and no other element owns it. **Management** covers the construction period and not only the operating life, because construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline decide how much of the starting soil survives to be managed at all (§4.2). Both widenings were forced by a decision that would otherwise have had nowhere to go, which is the useful kind of correction for a set like this to receive.

One decision genuinely sits outside the five, and it is the size of the project. Somebody chooses to build five megawatts rather than eighty, and that choice is real, but it is the choice that settles how much of each element is left. That is why it is not an element and why the [scale transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd) is the next chapter rather than a sixth row in the table.

The set would be wrong in either of two ways, and both are worth watching for. A decision that lands in none of the five would mean the list is short. A decision that lands in all five would mean the categories are not cutting anything. Neither has turned up yet, and a counterexample of either kind is among the more useful things this chapter could be sent (§8).
